## What The Business Is

Texas Instruments is a Dallas-based semiconductor company focused on **analog** and **embedded processing** chips. Its strategy centers on in-house manufacturing/technology, a broad catalog, direct market channels, and long-lived customer/product positions; in 2025, embedded processing was about 15% of revenue, with the broader business focused on analog and embedded products. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/97476/000009747626000059/txn-20251231.htm?utm_source=openai))

## What It Does

TI’s chips help electronic systems **manage power, sense and transmit real-world signals, and provide control/processing** in customer designs. The company serves industrial, automotive, personal electronics, communications equipment, and enterprise/data-center-related markets, with a portfolio of 80,000+ products. ([ti.com](https://www.ti.com/about-ti.html?utm_source=openai)) Its model emphasizes internal 300mm manufacturing, which management says supports competitive lead times, cycle flexibility, and long-term cost structure.

## Recent Highlights (Positive)

In Q1 2026, TI reported **$4.83 billion revenue**, **$1.55 billion net income**, and **$1.68 EPS**; the transcript excerpt says revenue rose **9% sequentially** and **19% year over year**, with Analog up **22% YoY** and Embedded Processing up **12% YoY**. ([ti.gcs-web.com](https://ti.gcs-web.com/static-files/b6565bf6-eef3-4a50-a12a-cce6cc24611b?utm_source=openai)) Management highlighted broad recovery signals: industrial revenue increased more than **30% YoY** and more than **20% sequentially**, data center grew about **90% YoY**, and communications equipment grew about **25% YoY**. The company guided Q2 2026 revenue to **$5.0 billion–$5.4 billion** and EPS to **$1.77–$2.05**, implying continued sequential growth from Q1. ([simplywall.st](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/semiconductors/nasdaq-txn/texas-instruments/news/texas-instruments-txn-is-up-75-after-strong-q2-ai-demand-gui/amp?utm_source=openai))

TI also continued to benefit from U.S. manufacturing investments: the transcript says trailing-12-month free cash flow rose to **$4.4 billion**, including **$965 million of CHIPS Act incentives**, with a **$555 million** payment tied to start of production at its newest Sherman, Texas 300mm wafer fab. The Sherman fab began production before the 90-day window but remains relevant because Q1 cash flow included the incentive payment and management described capacity/inventory as supporting a wide range of upturn scenarios. ([tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/new-texas-instruments-fab-will-pump-out-tens-of-millions-of-chips-per-day-first-300mm-fab-starts-production-after-usd60-billion-investment?utm_source=openai)) Silicon Labs shareholders also approved TI’s proposed acquisition in late April, moving the $7.5 billion embedded wireless connectivity deal one step forward. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/sec-filings/silicon-laboratories-shareholders-approve-merger-with-texas-instruments-93CH-4650286?utm_source=openai))

## Recent Highlights (Negative)

Management repeatedly cautioned that the strong industrial recovery may not yet be fully proven: the transcript notes macro/geopolitical uncertainty, a prior “head-fake” analog recovery pattern, and the need to see whether Q2 demand is sustainable. Automotive was comparatively less robust: Q1 automotive was only mid-single-digit YoY and roughly flat sequentially, with China down while the rest of world was up.

The Silicon Labs transaction adds execution, financing, and regulatory risk. TI’s own deal announcement lists risks including failure to obtain required approvals, disruption to operations and relationships, retention issues, litigation, unexpected costs, and potential deal delays or termination. ([ti.com](https://www.ti.com/about-ti/newsroom/news-releases/2026/2026-02-04-texas-instruments-to-acquire-silicon-labs.html?HQS=corp-dbwti-ep-tisi-bhp-news-null-wwe&utm_source=openai)) Recent merger-control reporting also said China’s regulator had not yet formally accepted the merger filing as of June 11, 2026, indicating a remaining regulatory gating item. ([mlex.com](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/mergers-acquisitions/articles/2488396/texas-instruments-silicon-labs-merger-filing-not-yet-accepted-in-china?utm_source=openai)) S&P affirmed TI’s rating but framed the deal as debt-funded and noted deleveraging expectations after the Silicon Labs acquisition, highlighting balance-sheet considerations around the $7.5 billion purchase. ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/-/view/type/HTML/id/3517729?utm_source=openai))

## Transcript Read — Long Case

- Industrial revenue up >30% YoY and >20% seq, broad across sectors, regions, and customer sizes
- Data center revenue up ~90% YoY and >25% seq, unique portfolio and capacity advantage
- Q2 guidance midpoint $5.2B implies ~8% seq growth, above typical seasonality
- Pricing flat in Q1 versus typical sequential decline; potential for increases in 2H if demand holds
- Inventory days down to 209, well-positioned to support demand; tightness in external assembly/test
- Free Cash Flow inflection: TTM FCF $4.4B, with path to >$8 per share in 2026 and upside from higher revenue
- SiLabs acquisition adds wireless connectivity and long-term growth at scale

Rationale: Industrial recovery is broad-based and still below prior peak, data center growth accelerating, strong Q2 guide above seasonal, pricing stabilizing with upside, and TXN's capacity advantage positions it for share gains.

## Bull Case
TXN is at the front end of a classic analog upcycle: Q1 2026 revenue +19% YoY with industrial +30% YoY (still ~15% below the 2022 peak), data center +90% YoY, and a Q2 guide (~$5.2B midpoint) above seasonality. Pricing was flat vs. the typical sequential decline, with possible increases in 2H. Critically, the multi-year capex wave (Sherman 300mm fabs) is cresting just as revenue reaccelerates — FCF has already inflected from $940M (2024 TTM) to $3.7B, with management pointing to >$8/share (~$7B+) in 2026, aided by CHIPS incentives. Silicon Labs adds embedded wireless connectivity scale. FCF could roughly double in 12 months even as EV grows only modestly.

## Bear Case
Automotive is flat sequentially with China down; last year's "head-fake" recovery pattern warns that the strong H1 may fade. The stock has already re-rated hard (market cap ~$267B vs. a 3-year mean of ~$174B), so much of the recovery and FCF inflection is priced in. The $7.5B debt-funded SiLabs deal adds regulatory (China filing not yet accepted), integration, and balance-sheet risk. Rising depreciation from the new fabs will weigh on margins, and if demand moderates, the optical multiple would need to compress violently to sustain today's EV.

## Multiple Re-Rating
- **Current implied multiple:** $277,431M EV / $3,721M TTM FCF ≈ **74.6x EV/FCF**
- **12-month forward multiple:** **44x**
- **Direction:** **CONTRACT**
- **Drivers:**
  1. **Capex normalization mechanically deflates the optical multiple.** Today's 74.6x reflects FCF suppressed by peak fab spend; as FCF roughly doubles toward the >$8/share path, the multiple must contract even if the stock is flat-to-up — this is normalization, not de-rating pessimism.
  2. **Recovery is substantially priced.** Market cap is ~53% above its 3-year mean; the broad industrial upturn and data-center growth are already in estimates, limiting further multiple support.
  3. **Second-derivative and deal risks cap premium.** YoY comps get harder in H2, auto/China remains soft, and the debt-funded SiLabs deal (with China approval pending) adds leverage — arguing for settling at a premium-but-not-extreme quality-analog multiple (~40–45x forward FCF), consistent with TXN's historical franchise premium.

## Logic
- **Forward FCF:** TTM FCF of $3,721M is inflecting sharply (from $1,455M a year ago). With revenue growing high-teens, capex rolling off, CHIPS incentives continuing, and management's >$8/share 2026 target (~$7.3B) as a ceiling, I forecast **$6,500M** forward FCF — strong growth but haircut for SiLabs integration costs, auto softness, and macro fade risk.
- **Forward EV:** $6,500M × 44x = **$286,000M**
- **EV-to-market-cap bridge:** current gap = $277,431.2M − $266,930.2M = $10,501M (net debt/other). Forward market cap = $286,000M − $10,501M ≈ **$275,499M**
- Implies ~3% upside to current market cap — the FCF doubling is largely offset by multiple normalization, i.e., the catalyst is mostly priced.

## Bull Case

TI's recovery is broad-based and durable: industrial revenue up >30% YoY (still 15% below 2022 peak, leaving room to run), data center up ~90% YoY on a secular AI build-out cycle where TXN's 300mm capacity and analog/embedded portfolio are structurally advantaged. The Sherman fab is now in production, meaning the multi-year capex wave that crushed FCF margins (TTM FCF troughed at $940M in mid-2024) is inflecting — FCF has already rebounded to $3,721M TTM and management guided to >$8/share FCF in 2026. Q2 guidance of $5.0–$5.4B is above typical seasonality, pricing has stabilized with potential upside in 2H, and inventory days have normalized to 209. The Silicon Labs acquisition adds embedded wireless connectivity at scale, expanding TXN's total addressable market and cross-sell potential.

## Bear Case

The current 74.6x EV/FCF multiple is artificially elevated by the capex trough and already discounts a substantial FCF recovery. The 3-year mean market cap is $174B; current market cap of $267B is 53% above that, embedding significant optimism. Automotive — historically a core growth engine — is flat sequentially with China declining, and management explicitly cautioned about a prior "head-fake" recovery pattern. The Silicon Labs deal adds $7.5B in debt-funded acquisition risk with China's regulator not yet accepting the merger filing as of June 11, 2026, creating closing uncertainty and balance-sheet pressure. Rising depreciation from the Sherman fab and integration costs from SiLabs will keep near-term FCF margins below historical norms (~30%+ FCF margin vs. current ~20%). Rates remain a headwind for duration-heavy equities.

## Multiple Re-Rating

- **Current implied multiple:** 74.6x EV/FCF ($277,431M EV / $3,721M TTM FCF)
- **12-month forward multiple:** 52.0x
- **Direction:** Contract
- **Top drivers:**
1. **FCF normalization mechanically compresses the optical multiple.** The 74.6x is a trough-FCF artifact; as the Sherman fab ramps to production and capex steps down, FCF inflects toward $4.9–5.5B and the denominator grows. Markets do not sustain trough multiples through normalization.
2. **Recovery is largely priced.** At 53% above the 3-year mean market cap, the stock already reflects the industrial/data-center rebound. The second derivative of growth is likely to moderate (industrial comps get tougher, data-center 90% YoY is unsustainable), limiting further multiple expansion.
3. **SiLabs integration risk and balance-sheet degradation.** Debt-funded $7.5B acquisition increases net debt, raises near-term OpEx/depreciation, and introduces regulatory closing risk (China). This argues for a risk premium that contracts the multiple.

A 52x multiple still represents a meaningful premium to TXN's pre-capex-wave historical range (~30–40x), reflecting genuine secular tailwinds (data center, SiLabs optionality) and TXN's manufacturing moat. But it acknowledges that the artificially inflated trough multiple cannot hold as FCF normalizes.

## Logic

**Forward FCF:** Base TTM FCF of $3,721M. Revenue is tracking toward ~$21B (15% growth from $18,438M TTM, supported by Q1 $4.83B + Q2 $5.2B midpoint guidance). As Sherman fab capex declines and CHIPS Act incentives continue (~$965M TTM), FCF margin expands from ~20% toward ~23–24%. Partially offset by SiLabs integration costs and higher depreciation. Forward FCF estimate: **$4,900M**.

**Forward EV:** $4,900M × 52.0x = **$254,800M**

**EV-to-MC bridge:** Current EV–MC gap = $277,431M − $266,930M = **$10,501M** (net debt). Forward: assume SiLabs closes in 6–9 months, adding ~$7.5B debt, partially offset by ~$4–5B FCF generation applied to deleveraging. Forward gap estimate: **~$15,000M**.

**Forward Market Cap:** $254,800M − $15,000M = **$239,800M**

This implies ~10% downside from current $266,930M, reflecting multiple compression that outweighs FCF growth — the classic pattern when trough multiples meet normalizing earnings power.

## Bull Case

TI's analog franchise is at the inflection point of a multi-quarter recovery. Industrial revenue up >30% YoY and still 15% below 2022 peak means there is meaningful runway. Data center growth at ~90% YoY introduces a secular demand layer that didn't meaningfully exist in prior cycles. The Sherman 300mm fab is now in production, meaning the capex wave that has depressed FCF for three years is cresting — TTM FCF has already inflected from $940M (2024) to $3,721M (2026), and with capex normalizing plus ~$965M of CHIPS Act incentives recurring, the path to $7-8B FCF in a fully recovered environment is credible. Pricing stabilized in Q1 (flat vs. typical seasonal decline), suggesting operating leverage as volume ramps. The Silicon Labs acquisition extends TI into embedded wireless connectivity, a strategic adjacency at scale.

## Bear Case

The stock is priced for perfection. Market cap of $267B sits 53% above the 3-year mean of $174B, and the current 74.5x EV/FCF multiple — even on depressed FCF — embeds aggressive assumptions about the pace and durability of recovery. Management itself flagged the "head-fake" analog recovery pattern from last year and cautioned on sustainability. Automotive was flat sequentially with China declining, a significant end-market underperforming. The $7.5B debt-funded Silicon Labs deal introduces execution risk, balance-sheet pressure (S&P noting deleveraging expectations), and an unresolved China regulatory filing as of June 2026. Rising depreciation from the fab ramp and acquisition-related OpEx will limit near-term margin expansion. If the industrial recovery moderates in H2 — as it did last year — the optical multiple compresses sharply.

## Multiple Re-Rating

**Current implied multiple:** 74.6x (EV $277,431M / TTM FCF $3,721M)

**Forward 12-month applied multiple:** 50.0x

**Direction:** Contract

**Top drivers:**
1. **FCF recovery is well-telegraphed and largely priced.** Management explicitly guided to >$8/share FCF in 2026; the market has already rallied the stock 53% above its 3-year mean on this thesis. The marginal buyer at these levels is paying for FCF growth that is already in guidance, not a surprise.
2. **Capex normalization is a mechanical story, not a re-rating catalyst.** The Sherman fab entering production is known and expected — it drives FCF up and the optical multiple down, but doesn't justify a higher *applied* multiple on forward FCF. The market rewards re-ratings for secular surprises, not cyclical capex timing that was guided years ago.
3. **Risk skew from deal execution and recovery durability.** The Silicon Labs integration (debt-funded, China regulatory gate unresolved) plus the prior-year head-fake pattern argue for multiple compression as a risk discount, even as fundamentals improve. The data-center growth narrative is exciting but is a small portion of revenue today and insufficient to offset the contraction from a 74.6x starting point.

## Logic

**Forward FCF estimate: $5,500M.** TTM FCF is $3,721M and inflecting sharply (from $940M two years ago). Revenue is tracking toward ~$20.5-21B (Q1 $4.83B + Q2 guide midpoint $5.2B implies ~$10B H1, with H2 seasonally similar or higher). Capex continues to decline as Sherman ramps to production. CHIPS Act incentives (~$965M TTM) recur. However, partial-year Silicon Labs integration costs and continued elevated depreciation from the fab ramp moderate the FCF recovery. A step from $3,721M to $5,500M represents ~48% growth — aggressive but supported by the revenue trajectory and capex taper.

**Forward EV:** 50.0x × $5,500M = $275,000M

**Forward market cap:** $275,000M − $10,501M = **$264,499M**
